argument: Simone de Beauvoir argues that meaning is created, not discovered, and that the discomfort driving philosophers to construct ethical systems throughout history is not meaninglessness but the ambiguity of existence: the fact that a person is simultaneously a subject and an object. Philosophers from Plato to Sartre have tried to resolve this discomfort dishonestly by favoring one side of a binary (subject over object, or vice versa) and subordinating the other. De Beauvoir insists an honest ethics must hold both sides in tension, and that real freedom requires willing the freedom of other people too, not just one's own.
keyIdeas: Just as someone might adopt a comforting religious story, someone can be drawn to total meaninglessness because it lets them avoid growing up and facing the moral weight of their own choices.

The discomfort that drives philosophers to build systems of meaning is not meaninglessness, per Cioran, but what de Beauvoir calls the ambiguity of existence: being pulled between polarities like subject and object that can never be reduced to one side.

Philosophers throughout history, including Plato, Descartes, Kant, and Sartre, have tried to resolve this discomfort by favoring one side of a binary opposition and subordinating the other side to it, rather than honestly holding both.

Femininity during de Beauvoir's lifetime was culturally defined around passivity and self-effacement, making women into objects while masculine traits were coded as active subjectivity, illustrating the real-world danger of favoring one side of the binary.

Real freedom requires willing the freedom of others, not just your own; treating people as mere objects, 'cogs in a machine,' is itself a denial of the ambiguity of existence and therefore not genuine freedom. Morality is created, not discovered, from within the ongoing discomfort of indefinite questioning.

terms.def: The state of being simultaneously subject and object, pulled between binary polarities that can never be reduced to one side.
Subjects act freely upon the world; objects are inert, acted-upon entities. De Beauvoir argues every person is both at once.
De Beauvoir's work attempting to build an honest moral framework for both the subjective and objective realms of existence.
Two sides of the same coin: exercising subjective power (transcendence) only makes sense against the objective limits you're navigating (immanence).
